message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"1.13","text":"While I was saying these things and what followed from them, a great uproar arose among the crowds. Some, as though pitying Barnabas, took my side; but others, being foolish, fiercely gnashed their teeth at me. When evening had at last overtaken us, I took Barnabas by the hand and, though he was unwilling, forcibly led him to my house. There I made him stay, so that no one might lay hands on him. After remaining for a few days and instructing me in a few points concerning the true word (only a little, as was possible in a few days), he said that he was hastening to Judaea for the sake of the religious festival, since he wished thereafter to be with his own compatriots.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"συνήραντό μοι","chosen":"took my side","rationale":"The phrase denotes joining Clement in support of Barnabas rather than physically raising something with him."},{"source_quote":"δεινῶς κατ’ ἐμοῦ ἔβρυχον τοὺς ὀδόντας","chosen":"fiercely gnashed their teeth at me","rationale":"Preserves the hostile bodily image and the direction of the hostility."},{"source_quote":"τοῦ ἀληθοῦς λόγου","chosen":"concerning the true word","rationale":"Retains λόγος as “word” without replacing the author’s expression with a later doctrinal formula."},{"source_quote":"ὀλίγον ὡς ἐν ὀλίγαις ἡμέραις","chosen":"only a little, as was possible in a few days","rationale":"Conveys the parenthetical qualification that the instruction was necessarily limited by the short time."},{"source_quote":"τῆς κατὰ τὴν θρησκείαν ἑορτῆς","chosen":"the religious festival","rationale":"Conveys a festival associated with religious observance without specifying a festival not named by the source."},{"source_quote":"τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ ὁμοεθνέσιν","chosen":"with his own compatriots","rationale":"ὁμοεθνής identifies people of the same nation or ethnic community."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"1.14","text":"But I could plainly see that he had grown weary. For when I said, “Only set out for me the words you heard from the man who appeared, and I, after embellishing them with discourse of my own, will proclaim God’s will. Then, in this way, within a few days I will sail with you—for I greatly long to be in the regions of Judaea—and perhaps I will even live with you for the whole course of my life,” he heard this and replied, “If you want to investigate our affairs and learn what is beneficial, sail with me immediately. At any rate, today I will tell you the directions to my dwelling and what you want to know, so that whenever you wish, you may come to us; for tomorrow I will depart for my own place.” Then, seeing that he could not be persuaded, I went with him as far as the harbor. After learning from him the directions to the dwellings that he had mentioned, I said to him, “Were it not that tomorrow I am collecting something owed to me, I would sail with you immediately. Nevertheless, I will catch up with you very soon.” After saying this and commending him to those in charge of the ship, I turned back grieving, remembering my good and intimate friend.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀποναρκήσας","chosen":"had grown weary","rationale":"The verb literally suggests becoming numb or listless; in context it describes Barnabas’s evident weariness with further delay."},{"source_quote":"τῷ ἐμῷ κοσμήσας λόγῳ","chosen":"after embellishing them with discourse of my own","rationale":"κοσμέω here describes Clement’s proposed rhetorical adornment of the words he received."},{"source_quote":"ἱστορῆσαι τὰ ἡμέτερα","chosen":"to investigate our affairs","rationale":"ἱστορέω denotes learning through inquiry, not merely writing a history."},{"source_quote":"ἐξ αὐτῆς","chosen":"immediately","rationale":"The elliptical idiom means from that very moment or straightaway."},{"source_quote":"ἐπεί γε τὰ σημεῖα τῆς οἰκήσεώς μου καὶ ὧν θέλεις ἐγώ σοι σήμερον ἐρῶ","chosen":"At any rate, today I will tell you the directions to my dwelling and what you want to know","rationale":"The clause is somewhat elliptical: ἐπεί γε marks a qualification after the preceding command, while ὧν θέλεις is understood as what Clement wishes to know."},{"source_quote":"ἐπιστῇς ἡμῖν","chosen":"you may come to us","rationale":"The verb here denotes arriving and presenting oneself where Barnabas and his associates are."},{"source_quote":"ἀδυσώπητον","chosen":"he could not be persuaded","rationale":"The adjective describes someone unyielding and unmoved by entreaty."},{"source_quote":"ἐπὶ τὰ ἐμαυτοῦ","chosen":"for my own place","rationale":"The substantival phrase is contextually elliptical and may denote one’s home, people, or affairs; “my own place” preserves that breadth."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"1.15","text":"After lingering for days and being unable to receive the debt in full, for the sake of speed I disregarded the remainder as an impediment and myself sailed away to Judaea. In fifteen days I reached Caesarea of Strato. Once I had set foot on land and was seeking lodging, I learned that a certain man named Peter, the most highly regarded disciple of the man who had appeared in Judaea and had performed signs and wonders, was to hold a verbal debate the next day with Simon the Samaritan from Gittha. When I heard this, I asked that his lodging be pointed out to me; and duly I learned it and stood at the gateway. When those in the house saw me, they questioned me about who I was and where I had come from. And behold, Barnabas came out and, as soon as he saw me, embraced me, rejoicing greatly and weeping. Taking me by the hand, he led me in to where Peter was and said to me, “This is Peter, whom I declared to you to be greatest in the wisdom of God. I spoke to him about you without ceasing, as you will learn of your own accord, for I truthfully set before him all the good things concerning you. At the same time I also disclosed your intention, so that he himself longs to see you too. Therefore, through my own hands, I present you to him as a great gift.” After saying this and presenting me, he said, “This is Clement, Peter.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὸ χρέος οὐχ. ὅλον λαβεῖν","chosen":"being unable to receive the debt in full","rationale":"The translation construes οὐχ with ὅλον despite the intervening printed full stop, which is disclosed under source issues."},{"source_quote":"Καισάρειαν κατήντησα τὴν Στράτωνος","chosen":"I reached Caesarea of Strato","rationale":"Preserves the distinguishing genitive Στράτωνος rather than reducing the place-name to Caesarea."},{"source_quote":"ζήτησιν ποιεῖται λόγων","chosen":"was to hold a verbal debate","rationale":"The expression denotes an organized inquiry or dispute conducted through words."},{"source_quote":"καὶ ὁμῶς ἔμαθον","chosen":"and duly I learned it","rationale":"The uncommon adverb ὁμῶς can convey correspondence or like manner; “duly” gives it a modest discourse function without silently changing it to ὅμως."},{"source_quote":"ἀντέβαλλον τίς τε ὢν καὶ πόθεν ἥκω","chosen":"they questioned me about who I was and where I had come from","rationale":"In this context ἀντιβάλλω introduces inquiry concerning Clement’s identity and origin."},{"source_quote":"ᾧ ἀπαύστως σε ἀντέβαλλον","chosen":"I spoke to him about you without ceasing","rationale":"Here the verb concerns repeatedly setting information about Clement before Peter."},{"source_quote":"ὡς εἴσει ἐκ ταὐτομάτου","chosen":"as you will learn of your own accord","rationale":"ἐκ ταὐτομάτου indicates discovery directly or for oneself."},{"source_quote":"ὅτι πάντα τὰ κατὰ σὲ καλὰ ὄντα ἀψευδῶς ἀντέβαλλον","chosen":"for I truthfully set before him all the good things concerning you","rationale":"The repeated verb is rendered as presenting a report, while ἀψευδῶς explicitly characterizes it as truthful."},{"source_quote":"ὡς αὐτὸν γλίχεσθαι καὶ ἰδεῖν σε","chosen":"so that he himself longs to see you too","rationale":"The rendering takes αὐτόν as the subject of the infinitival construction and σε as the object of ἰδεῖν."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"τὸ χρέος οὐχ. ὅλον λαβεῖν δυνηθείς","issue":"The supplied print places a full stop after οὐχ, interrupting the syntactically expected phrase οὐχ ὅλον. The translation treats this as a nonblocking printed punctuation defect, not as a transcription error.","proposed_reading":"τὸ χρέος οὐχ ὅλον λαβεῖν δυνηθείς","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"τοῦ ἐν Ἰουδαίᾳ εἰσφανέντος ἀνδρὸς τοῦ σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα· πεποιηκότος ὁ δοκιμώτατος ὑπάρχων μαθητής","issue":"The printed high point after τέρατα separates the object phrase from πεποιηκότος, although the genitive participle most naturally modifies ἀνδρός. The translation follows that continuous construction while preserving the supplied wording.","proposed_reading":"τοῦ ἐν Ἰουδαίᾳ εἰσφανέντος ἀνδρὸς τοῦ σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα πεποιηκότος, ὁ δοκιμώτατος ὑπάρχων μαθητής","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"1.16","text":"Good Peter sprang forward as soon as he heard the name and kissed me warmly. After making me sit down, he immediately said, “You did well when you magnanimously welcomed Barnabas, the herald of truth, in honor of the God who truly is, neither being ashamed nor fearing the anger of the uneducated crowds. You will be blessed. For just as you welcomed the ambassador of truth with every honor, so Truth herself will make you, though a stranger to her own city, a citizen of it. Then you will rejoice greatly because you have now lent a brief kindness (speaking of a disposition toward good words). You will be an heir to eternal and inalienable good things. Do not tire yourself setting your character before me, for truthful Barnabas has set before us everything about you, making favorable mention of you nearly every day. And, to tell you briefly as a genuine friend the matter at hand, if nothing hinders you, travel with us, partaking of the discourses of truth that I intend to deliver from city to city, as far as Rome itself. And as for you, if there is anything you want, say it.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"μεγαλοφρόνως","chosen":"magnanimously","rationale":"The adverb describes Clement’s noble or high-minded courage in receiving Barnabas."},{"source_quote":"τοῦ ὄντως θεοῦ","chosen":"the God who truly is","rationale":"Preserves the force of ὄντως rather than reducing the expression to the conventional title “the true God.”"},{"source_quote":"αὐτή σε ἡ ἀλήθεια","chosen":"Truth herself","rationale":"Retains the source’s emphatic personification of feminine ἀλήθεια."},{"source_quote":"βραχεῖαν νῦν ἐδάνεισας χάριν","chosen":"you have now lent a brief kindness","rationale":"Preserves the lending metaphor and the likely temporal contrast between the limited kindness and lasting good things."},{"source_quote":"προαίρεσιν λόγων καλῶν λέγων","chosen":"speaking of a disposition toward good words","rationale":"The parenthetical phrase explains the preceding kindness through προαίρεσις, though the exact relationship between the disposition and “good words” remains compressed."},{"source_quote":"ἀιδίων καὶ ἀναφαιρέτων ἀγαθῶν","chosen":"eternal and inalienable good things","rationale":"ἀναφαίρετος describes what cannot be taken away; “good things” retains the substantival plural without adding a specific doctrinal category."},{"source_quote":"μὴ κάμνε ἀντιβάλλειν μοι τὸ σὸν ἦθος","chosen":"Do not tire yourself setting your character before me","rationale":"The expression tells Clement not to labor at presenting or explaining his character to Peter."},{"source_quote":"τὴν ἀγαθήν σου ποιούμενος μνήμην","chosen":"making favorable mention of you","rationale":"The idiom denotes repeatedly remembering or mentioning Clement favorably."},{"source_quote":"τὸ προκείμενον","chosen":"the matter at hand","rationale":"The phrase refers to the proposal or course presently being placed before Clement."},{"source_quote":"μεταλαμβάνων τῶν τῆς ἀληθείας λόγων","chosen":"partaking of the discourses of truth","rationale":"μεταλαμβάνω presents Clement as sharing in or receiving the discourses, not necessarily as their speaker."},{"source_quote":"ὧν κατὰ πόλιν ποιεῖσθαι μέλλω μέχρι Ῥώμης αὐτῆς","chosen":"that I intend to deliver from city to city, as far as Rome itself","rationale":"ποιεῖσθαι λόγους means to give or conduct discourses, while κατὰ πόλιν marks their repeated delivery in successive cities."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
